newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Gold - Strong physical demand supports rally.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Strong physical demand supports rally.

text.p: Physical gold demand in Asia should remain strong over the next week until possibly the end of the month, underpinning the recent rally, but the longer-term price outlook remains bearish, dealers said on Friday.

"I think demand will remain good," a dealer for a North American bank in Singapore said, adding brisk buying will keep the yellow metal firmly supported above US$340 an ounce. "Demand in Asia right now is very strong."

Hong Kong spot gold opened slightly above New York's overnight close on Friday at $340.90/$341.40 an ounce. On Wednesday, bullion staged a blistering rally gaining $10 an ounce in an hour as it rebounded from 3-1/4-year lows.
"The Malays and the Chinese are buying. In fact, everybody is buying. Demand should remain firm until the end of February," another Singapore dealer said.
Purchasing picked up strongly ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year period, which was celebrated on February 7 and 8, and should continue over the next two weeks, traders said.
Buyers in Indonesia and Malaysia were purchasing gold ahead of the Hari Raya celebrations on February 9. Demand from India and Pakistan also remains robust, they added.
The strong demand and tigh supplies have boosted gold premiums across Asia.

Singapore premiums were quoted steady to slightly higher by traders at around 150 U.S. cents an ounce over London spot prices, while Hong Kong premiums were indicated at anything from 125 cents to as high as 170 cents.
"The premiums are up mostly because of strong demand all around," a Singapore dealer said. "It should stay that way for the time being."
But one Hong Kong dealer said: "The premium can go as high as you like, but if the gold isn't there, it means nothing, you still can't sell it," he said.
Further short-covering in Asia could push spot gold prices closer to $350-$355 an ounce.
"You're going to see strong selling once we hit that level," a dealer said.
On the downside, support was pegged at the previous resistance level around $340-$342.

Over the longer term most dealers remain pessimistic about the resilience of the gold price saying the continued strength of Wall Street and local regional bourses is likely to siphon money out of the precious metals complex.
"Gold has been hit terribly by all these surging stock markets," a Singapore dealer said. "If things don't change, you should see gold slowly drift lower next month."
"Dealer sentiment is still a bit bearish," a Hong Kong dealer said, adding the market's wariness was related to word last week of central banks sales.

Producers, too, had sold quite heavily last week, dealers in the colony said, moving significant quantities into the market, pressured by movements of the Australian dollar and the South African Rand.
The closer the gold price moves to $300, seen by some dealing sources as the cut-off point for covering the majority of producer costs, the more uncomfortable the mines become, another dealer said.
"Even as it gets to $335, $330, they will be very edgy," the European bank dealer said.
"Normally they are greedy and when they see it (the price) move up they will hold back and see what happens first.
"Since November or December, we have been actively waiting for the funds to short cover, they've been short for a long, long time and they are very well in the money," another Hong Kong dealer said.
"We haven't really believed in this rally, because we have been disappointed many times now... we have given back more than we gained."
Another dealer saw 1997 dominated by the appreciation of the U.S. dollar and described the picture for bullion as "disappointing... depressing."
-- Rene Pastor, Singapore newroom, +65 870-3174
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom, +86 21 6279-7004
